title: Reversible reactions and extent
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:36Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-02T04:35:39Z autoreview: cleared with the fix (card wording)

match.reason: The bank's static and dynamic equilibrium point covers reversibility and closed systems but does not teach the distinction between rate and extent, which the new point is about, and the rates point covers only rate, so no existing point fits exactly or with small changes.

draft.title: Reversible reactions and extent
card: In a reversible reaction, the products can react to form the reactants again. It is shown with a double arrow, such as N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g). The forward reaction goes left to right and the reverse reaction goes right to left.
how fast a reaction goes, or how quickly reactants are used up or products form.
how far a reaction goes, or how much of the reactants have turned into products when the reaction stops changing.

In a reversible reaction, the reactants do not all turn into products, so the extent is less than complete. A catalyst or a higher temperature can make a reaction faster. That is a change in rate, not a direct statement about extent.
draft.remember: Rate is how fast. Extent is how far. They are different things.

a.q: Which statement describes the extent of a reaction?
opts: How much reactant has become product by the end
How quickly the reactants are used up at the start
How much energy is needed to start the reaction
How much faster the reaction goes with a catalyst
a.why: Extent is about how far the reaction goes, which means how much reactant has turned into product. The option about reactants being used up quickly describes rate, which is a different idea.
a.clue: Extent asks how far, not how fast.

b.q: Ava runs a reversible reaction at two temperatures. At the higher temperature, the mixture stops changing after 2 minutes. At the lower temperature, it takes 10 minutes. What can she say from this alone?
opts: The reaction is faster at the higher temperature
The reaction goes further at the higher temperature
The reaction is faster at the lower temperature
The reaction goes further at the lower temperature
b.why: Stopping changing sooner shows the reaction is faster at the higher temperature, which is about rate. The time taken does not show how much product formed, so nothing can be said about extent from this alone.
b.clue: Time taken tells you about rate, not about how far.

a.best: How much reactant has become product by the end

b.best: The reaction is faster at the higher temperature

problems.detail: The card groups 'a catalyst or a higher temperature' together, then says this is 'a change in rate, not a direct statement about extent'. For a catalyst that is right. But changing temperature does change the extent of a reversible reaction by shifting the equilibrium position. Students may come away thinking temperature, like a catalyst, affects only rate. The point about rate should be limited to the catalyst, or the card should say that temperature can also change extent, without teaching Le Chatelier here.

check.summary: Both questions and their answers are sound. One card line puts temperature with catalysts as affecting only rate, which could mislead students, because temperature also changes extent in reversible reactions.

proposal.title: Reversible reactions and extent
card: In a reversible reaction, the products can react to form the reactants again. It is shown with a double arrow, such as N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g), with the forward reaction going left to right and the reverse going right to left.
how fast a reaction goes, or how quickly reactants are used up or products form. A faster reaction reaches the point where it stops changing sooner.
how far a reaction goes, or how much of the reactants have turned into products when the reaction stops changing.

In a reversible reaction, the reactants do not all turn into products, so the extent is incomplete. A catalyst changes the rate but not the extent, while a change in temperature can change both. Knowing one does not tell you the other.
